summary: This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for SNMP to configure, monitor, and control routers running VRRPv3 for IPv4 and IPv6, as defined in RFC 5798. It obsoletes RFC 2787.

eli5.summary: VRRP lets backup routers take over when the main one fails. This is a standard list of dials and gauges so network tools can check and change those settings.

subtitle: The SNMP MIB that lets management tools configure and monitor VRRPv3 routers over IPv4 and IPv6.

tldr.problem: Routers that use VRRPv3 to back each other up need a standard way for management systems to configure, monitor and control them over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The VRRPV3-MIB module defines three tables (operations, statistics and associated addresses) plus two notifications, indexed by interface, VRID and IP version, so IPv4 and IPv6 virtual routers are separate rows.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6527 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2787, updating the MIB for VRRPv3 as defined in RFC 5798 and for current MIB conventions.

today: RFC 6527 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012. It obsoletes RFC 2787, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
This specification defines a part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for SNMP-based network management. It defines objects for configuring, monitoring and controlling routers that run the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol Version 3 (VRRPv3) for both IPv4 and IPv6, as defined in RFC 5798.

The module is written in SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579, RFC 2580) and sits inside the Internet-Standard Management Framework described in RFC 3410. It obsoletes RFC 2787. The major changes follow the protocol changes between RFC 2338 and RFC 5798, and the module is brought up to current MIB conventions.
sections.eli5: This RFC is a shared list of questions a network tool can ask a backup-capable router, and settings it can change.

sections.title: Design: Indexing and Multi-Stack Handling
sections.content:
A router may run VRRP on several interfaces, so the tables use ifIndex from the IF-MIB (RFC 2863) as an index. The module supports multi-stack implementations that run VRRP over both IPv4 and IPv6, and rows are identified by the IP version, the Virtual Router Identifier (VRID) and the ifIndex.

The RFC records that reviewers found different possible interpretations of RFC 5798, and the VRRP working group could not agree on one. This document therefore assumes that IPv4 and IPv6 virtual routers are two separate logical entities, each with its own row in vrrpv3OperationsTable, because the protocol's behavior in a multi-stack scenario is undefined.

An example network shows two VRRP routers, VR1 and VR2, each running two virtual routers (VRID 1 and 2) with IPv4 and IPv6 rows. A priority of 255 in the operations table marks the router that owns the address, and State shows Master or Backup.
sections.eli5: Each pair of address type and virtual router number gets its own line in the list, so the IPv4 backup job and the IPv6 backup job never get mixed up.

sections.title: The Three Tables
sections.content:
The module contains three tables. vrrpv3OperationsTable holds the operational characteristics, with one row per virtual router. vrrpv3StatisticsTable holds operating statistics and augments the operations entry. vrrpv3AssociatedIpAddrTable lists the addresses a virtual router backs up.

Key columns in the operations table include the master's real address (vrrpv3OperationsMasterIpAddr), the primary address, the virtual MAC address, the state, the priority, the advertisement interval, the preempt mode, the accept mode and the uptime. The VRID textual convention is an integer from 1 to 255. The address type supports only ipv4(1) and ipv6(2).

Priority is used in master election, where higher means preferred; it defaults to 100. A priority of 0 is sent by a master that has stopped participating, and 255 belongs to the address owner, so agents should reject setting either value. The advertisement interval is in centiseconds, ranges from 1 to 4095 and defaults to 100, and only the master sends advertisements. Preempt mode defaults to true, and accept mode, which applies to IPv6 only, defaults to false.
sections.eli5: One table says how each backup router is set up, one counts what happened, and one lists the addresses it is protecting.

sections.title: Creating and Removing Rows
sections.content:
Rows are managed with the SNMP RowStatus convention. A new operations row must start with status initialize(1) and cannot move to backup or master until its row status is active(1). A row cannot become active until the address type, VRID and primary address are set and at least one active row exists in the associated address table.

The RFC gives a typical order to add a virtual router: create the operations row with createAndWait(5), create one or more associated address rows, fill in the operations entry, then set the row status to active(1). To delete, set the operations row to notInService(2), destroy the associated address rows, then destroy the operations row. Changes to these tables are persistent, and the entity SHOULD save them to non-volatile storage. Associated address rows cannot be modified unless the virtual router has transitioned to initialize(1), and implementations should not delete the last address row of an active virtual router.
sections.eli5: To add a backup job you fill in the form first and flip the switch last. To remove one, you switch it off first and then erase the pieces.

sections.title: Statistics and Notifications
sections.content:
Three router-wide counters track packets with a bad checksum, an unsupported version or an unknown VRID, together with a discontinuity timestamp. Each virtual router also has per-row counters for master transitions, received advertisements, advertisement interval errors, IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit not equal to 255, priority-zero packets sent and received, invalid type, address list mismatches and short packets. A refresh rate object reports the minimum reasonable polling interval in milliseconds.

Two notifications are defined. vrrpv3NewMaster tells a manager that the sending agent became master and carries the master address and the reason. vrrpv3ProtoError reports a protocol error and carries its reason. They are controlled with the mechanisms of RFC 3413.
sections.eli5: The router keeps score of mistakes it saw and can ring a bell when it becomes the boss router or something goes wrong.

sections.title: Compliance Statements
sections.content:
Two compliance levels are defined. vrrpv3FullCompliance requires the operations, statistics, info and notifications groups and says settable priority values are 1 to 254. vrrpv3ReadOnlyCompliance lets an implementation skip write support for priority, primary address, advertisement interval, preempt mode, accept mode and the two row status objects, so the device can be monitored but not configured with this MIB.

The module is registered as { mib-2 207 }. IANA has deprecated value 68 under mib-2, which was assigned to the old VRRP-MIB.
sections.eli5: A device can promise to do everything, including changing settings, or promise only to let you look at the gauges.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Several objects are read-write or read-create, and misuse can hurt the network. The RFC names examples: an unauthorized priority change can make the wrong router master; a changed primary address could give the new master an incorrect address; a malicious advertisement interval could flood the network or make the master advertise too rarely; and the row status object could be used to disable a virtual router.

Implementations MUST provide the SNMPv3 security features described in RFC 3410, including authentication and privacy through USM (RFC 3414) with AES (RFC 3826), and MAY also support the Transport Security Model with SSH or TLS/DTLS. Deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. The operator remains responsible for giving access only to legitimate users.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can change these settings can mess up which router is in charge, so only trusted people, with proper locks, should be allowed to.

viz.caption: OBJECT TREE OF THE VRRPV3-MIB MODULE (RFC 6527)

items.label: initialize
items.desc: The virtual router is waiting for a startup event.

items.label: backup
items.desc: The virtual router is monitoring the availability of the master.

items.label: master
items.desc: The virtual router is forwarding packets for its associated IP addresses.

items.label: notMaster
items.desc: The virtual router never became master.

items.label: preempted
items.desc: Became master by preempting another router.

items.label: masterNoResponse
items.desc: Became master because the master did not respond.
